title: Genetic Algorithm
body:
Optimisation by breeding. Keep a **population** of candidate solutions, score each one, let the
better ones have more children, and repeat. It is natural selection run as an algorithm, and it
applies where you can *score* an answer but cannot *differentiate* one.

```
population ← N random candidates
repeat:
    score every candidate with the fitness function
    select parents, weighted by fitness
    crossover pairs of parents to make children
    mutate children with small probability
    population ← the children (plus the best few parents, usually)
until fitness stops improving or the budget runs out
```

## The five pieces

| Piece | Job | Where it goes wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **Representation** | encode a candidate as a string, list, or tree | a bad encoding makes crossover produce nonsense |
| **Fitness function** | one number, higher is better | the only thing the algorithm knows; it optimises this, not what you meant |
| **Selection** | fitter parents reproduce more (tournament, roulette) | too greedy and the population converges early |
| **Crossover** | combine two parents into a child | the mechanism that actually *combines* good ideas |
| **Mutation** | random small change | too little and it stalls; too much and it is a random walk |

**Crossover is what makes it a genetic algorithm** rather than parallel random restarts. The bet
is that two solutions good for different reasons can be spliced into one good for both, and that
bet only pays off if the representation puts related decisions next to each other.

**Mutation is what escapes local optima**, and that is the interesting contrast with the rest of
the course.

## Against gradient descent

[[Gradient Descent]] follows the slope downhill. It needs a differentiable landscape, it moves one
point, and it stops at whatever [[Optimization|local minimum]] it fell into.

| | [[Gradient Descent]] | Genetic algorithm |
|---|---|---|
| Needs | a derivative | a fitness number, nothing else |
| Maintains | one point | a population |
| Escapes local optima | no, not on its own | yes, by mutation and diversity |
| Guarantees | converges on convex problems | **none whatsoever** |
| Good for | smooth continuous problems | discrete, combinatorial, black-box, ugly |

So the choice is not really a contest. Use gradients where the landscape has them, which is why
[[Neural Network]] training is gradient descent and not evolution. Use a GA for scheduling,
routing, circuit layout, and antenna shapes: problems where "nudge the parameters slightly"
is not even meaningful. See [[Multivariable Optimization]] for the calculus version of the
same question.

**It is a local search, not a search.** Nothing here builds a path or explores a graph the way
[[Best-First Search]] does. There is no notion of a route to the answer, only better and worse
answers, which is why it sits in this block as the alternative rather than a variant.
